## **Project Overview**

Analyzed Montgomery County, Maryland crime data alongside statewide crime statistics and Census population data to evaluate how the county's public safety compares with other Maryland jurisdictions. The analysis examines crime trends from 1975 through 2020 and compares raw crime counts with population-adjusted rates to determine whether Montgomery County is a relatively safe place to live. The findings provide context for public safety planning and resource allocation.

## Introduction

For this research project, we will determine if Montgomery County,
Maryland (MOCO) is a safe place to live. This will be accomplished by
analyzing crime statistics from various data sources.

Collecting this data will help us understand the prevalence of different
types of crime within a specific area. Homes in areas where crime is
high tend to cost less because of the increased risks involved as well
as the decrease in quality of life. Therefore, MOCO was chosen to
determine if I, the writer, would be wise to purchase a home within its
boundaries.

This study is a data science problem because crime statistics are
quantitative evidence collected by scientific research that can show the
areas where there are high incidents of crime activities and the trends
that exist over time.

## II. Research Questions

This research paper will cover some exploratory data analysis,
transformations, and summary statistics of the levels of safety within
MOCO so that safety can be determined. Therefore, we will focus on the
following research questions:

1.  How do we define safety?
2.  How much crime is there?

<!-- -->

a.  Total number of incidents by city within MOCO
b.  Incidents per capita

<!-- -->

3.  What are the types of crimes?
4.  How crime within MOCO compares to other areas.
5.  How MOCO crime rates compare to the National crime statistics.
6.  How does crime trend over time?
7.  Based on population trends, are people moving to or away from MOCO?


## III. Approach

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) was used to examine reported crime
patterns in Montgomery County, Maryland. R was used to clean,
combine, and analyze crime records from multiple sources and produce
visual summaries of the findings.

The analysis examines reported crime volumes, historical trends,
and comparisons with other jurisdictions. Population data was
incorporated to calculate per capita crime rates, allowing
comparisons that account for differences in population size.

## IV. How the Approach Addresses the Problem

The analysis addressed whether MOCO is a safe place to live in several ways. A map of reported incidents shows where crime occurs across the county. Bar charts compare total crime and crime per capita across Maryland counties, and a scatterplot places Montgomery County among counties nationwide by population and total crime. Line charts show how the county's crime totals and crime rate per 100,000 people changed from 1975 through 2020. A scatterplot of census tracts shows how the number of crimes relates to population within the county.

## V. Data

The analysis uses four datasets containing reported crime incidents,
county-level crime statistics, historical crime trends, and population
estimates. Data preparation included standardizing location identifiers,
selecting relevant crime categories, and combining crime and population
information for comparison.

### Montgomery County Crime Data

Source: [Montgomery County Open Data](https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/?groups=local&organization=montgomery-county-of-maryland&tags=district)

The `1-Crime Reset.csv` dataset contains the 35,460 crime incidents
reported in Montgomery County in 2022. Its geographic information includes location coordinates and Census identifiers used to examine crime across
communities. The dataset was cleaned and supplemented with geographic
information to support location-based comparisons.

### United States Crime Rates by County

Source: [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mikejohnsonjr/united-states-crime-rates-by-county)

The `2-United States_crime_rates_by_county.csv` dataset contains
county-level crime statistics and population figures. It supports
comparisons between Montgomery County, other Maryland counties,
and jurisdictions nationwide.

### Montgomery County Historical Crime Data

Source: [Maryland Open Data](https://opendata.maryland.gov/Public-Safety/Violent-Crime-Property-Crime-by-County-1975-to-Pre/jwfa-fdxs/data)

The `3-Montgomery_County_Crime_by_year.csv` dataset contains annual
crime statistics from 1975 through 2020. It includes violent and
property crime totals, population figures, and crime rates per
100,000 residents. These records support the historical trend analysis.

### Montgomery County Census Tract Population

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2018–2022.

The `5-MOCO_Tract_Population_2022.csv` dataset contains population
estimates by Census tract within Montgomery County. Census tract
identifiers allow population estimates to be joined with geographically
referenced crime records for comparisons within the county.

The following R packages are used in this analysis:

# Part TWO

## I. Importing and Cleaning the Data

The four datasets were reviewed and prepared for analysis to ensure
consistent geographic identifiers, crime classifications, and
population comparisons.

**Data.1 — Montgomery County Crime Data**

The dataset contains 35,460 reported crime incidents from 2022.
Because block addresses and police districts were not precise enough
for geographic analysis, each record's latitude and longitude were
run through Geocodio, which added Census place names and Census tract
codes. Geocodio matched 35,102 records; the remaining 358 have no
tract information. The full Census tract code, which includes the
state and county FIPS codes, was converted into a GEOID field to
support comparisons with Census population data.

**Data.2 — United States Crime Rates by County**

A `total.crime` variable was calculated using eight crime
categories: murder, rape, robbery, aggravated assault, burglary,
larceny, motor vehicle theft, and arson. A `Distinguish` variable
was also created to identify Montgomery County in visual
comparisons with other jurisdictions.

**Data.3 — Montgomery County Historical Crime Data**

This dataset required no additional modifications. Its annual
crime totals, population figures, and crime rates support the
historical analysis from 1975 through 2020.

**New.Data.4 — Montgomery County Census Tract Population**

Population estimates from the 2018–2022 American Community Survey
were saved locally as `5-MOCO_Tract_Population_2022.csv`.
GEOID is read as text so that these population estimates can be
joined with the geographically referenced crime records in Data.1.

```{r Libraries, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#This is where the packages are loaded and chunk options are set.
#The CSV files must be in the same folder as this Rmd file.

library(readr)
require("knitr")

opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)

library(magick)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
```

## II. Look of Final Data Sets

The four datasets were prepared for analysis, with variables added
where necessary to support geographic comparisons and crime rate
calculations. Shared geographic identifiers allow crime records to
be connected with population and location information.

- **Data.1** contains 35,460 observations and 66 columns, including
  35,102 records with Census tract identifiers and 358 without.
- **Data.2** contains 3,136 observations and 26 columns after
  creating the `total.crime` and `Distinguish` variables.
- **Data.3** remains unchanged, with 46 observations and 31 columns.
- **New.Data.4** contains 232 observations and 5 columns, with GEOID
  preserved as text to support matching with Data.1.

```{r Final Datasets}
# Load Montgomery County crime records
Data.1 <- read.csv("1-Crime Reset.csv") %>%
  mutate(GEOID = as.character(Full.FIPS..tract.))

# Load county crime statistics and create comparison variables
Data.2 <- read.csv("2-United States_crime_rates_by_county.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    total.crime = MURDER + RAPE + ROBBERY + AGASSLT +
                  BURGLRY + LARCENY + MVTHEFT + ARSON,
    Distinguish = county_name == "Montgomery County, MD")

# Load historical Montgomery County crime data
Data.3 <- read.csv("3-Montgomery_County_Crime_by_year.csv")

# Load saved Census tract population estimates
New.Data.4 <- read.csv(
  "5-MOCO_Tract_Population_2022.csv",
  colClasses = c(GEOID = "character"))
```

## III. Not Self-Evident Information

The `Offence.Code` variable in Data.1 identifies different crime
classifications, but the meaning and criteria behind those codes are
not immediately apparent. For example, homicide classifications
distinguish between different circumstances and relationships involving
the individuals affected.

Understanding these distinctions could influence how someone evaluates
neighborhood safety. A person might assess crimes involving family
members differently from incidents involving strangers. However,
determining whether those distinctions are meaningful would require
additional information about how offenses are classified and recorded.

This analysis focuses on reported crime counts and rates rather than
interpreting the circumstances of individual incidents.

## IV. Different Ways to Look at the Data

The same data could be examined in several other ways to judge whether Montgomery County is a safe place to live. Incidents could be broken down by street or neighborhood to show where crime is most concentrated. Police district boundaries could be compared with population to see whether some districts serve too many residents to respond efficiently. The time of day or day of the week could show when crimes are most likely to occur. A reader might also focus on a single crime type; for example, someone might treat aggravated assaults as the main measure of safety and set other offenses aside.

The color-coded map below shows how widely reported incidents are spread across the county, which is why the same information can be divided and interpreted in so many ways.

```{r Visual of Crimes across County, out.width="95%"}
#This is a display that shows a conglomerate of crimes across the county

Crime.map <- image_read("Screenshotmoco.png")

Crime.map

```

*Screenshot of an online map of reported Montgomery County crime incidents. Base map © Mapbox © OpenStreetMap contributors.*

## V. Plan to Slice and Dice the Data

The county comparisons and historical trends define crime as violent and property crimes only. The county comparison uses murder, rape, robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, larceny, motor vehicle theft, and arson; the historical data uses the same categories except arson. Crimes against society, such as drug offenses, are not included in these measures.

The 2022 incident data (Data.1) includes all 35,460 reported incidents, including 5,307 crimes against society. The neighborhood table and the Census tract scatterplot therefore reflect all reported offenses, not only violent and property crimes.

Crime is also compared with population, because some areas have far fewer residents than others. Population-adjusted rates allow places of different sizes to be compared, and the historical data shows how Montgomery County's crime totals and rates changed from 1975 through 2020.

## VI. Summarizing Data to Answer Key Questions

The data was summarized to answer the key questions by illustrating
tables and plots that will allow the end-user to visualize patterns and
trends, and enable insights and correlations as it applies to safety
within the county.

## VIII. Plots and Tables to Illustrate Findings

```{r Table of Incidents by City}
#This is a table that lists incidents of crime for neighborhoods in the County 

Group.Place = Data.1 %>%
    group_by (Place.Name) %>%
    summarise(number.of.crime = n())
kable(Group.Place)
```

```{r Combine data for Population vs Crime by Town}
#This is a method that counts the number of crimes by neighborhood 
#according to the Census

Group.crime = Data.1 %>%
    group_by (GEOID) %>%
    summarise(number.of.crime = n())

#This combines crimes with the population using the census tract
Pop.Crime.by = left_join(Group.crime, New.Data.4, by="GEOID") 

```

```{r Plot Crime vs Town Population}
#This plots the crimes in relation to county population, which shows as 
#population rises, incidents in crime also rises
Pop.Crime.by %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x=estimate, y=number.of.crime)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    labs(title = "Crime and Population", y = "Number of Crimes", 
         x = "Population") +
    geom_point()
```

```{r Total Crime - Filtering to Maryland}
#Table of crime comparing counties all over Maryland.

Data.2 %>%
    filter(FIPS_ST == 24) %>%
    arrange(county_name) %>%
    select(county_name,population,total.crime)

```

```{r Incidents by City and MOCO comparison}
#This is a bar graph showing how Montgomery County crime numbers compares to 
#other counties in Maryland

Data.2 %>%
    filter(FIPS_ST == 24) %>% #this is the code for MD
    ggplot(aes(x=fct_reorder(county_name,total.crime), y=total.crime, fill = Distinguish)) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = "Total Crime by County in Maryland", y = "Crime", x = "County")
```

```{r Incident Comparison Per Capita}
#This is a bar chart of crime per capita for all Maryland counties and 
#highlights Montgomery County
Data.2 %>%
    filter(FIPS_ST == 24) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x=fct_reorder(county_name,total.crime/population), 
               y=total.crime/population, fill = Distinguish)) +
    geom_col() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = "Total Crime per Capita by County in Maryland", 
         y = "Crime", x = "County")
```

```{r Plot Crime vs County Population}
#This plots the population in relation to crime with Montgomery County in green.
#It shows that though Montgomery county with a high population has more 
#incidents than other counties, when compared to like-sized counties, the number 
#of crimes are low.
Data.2 %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x=log(population), y=log(total.crime), col=Distinguish)) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    labs(title = "Where Montgomery County lies in a Plot", y = "Crime", 
         x = "Population") +
    geom_point()

```

```{r Line Plot of County Crime Trend}
#Plots Montgomery county crime over time, showing a deep decline

Data.3 %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x=YEAR, y=GRAND.TOTAL)) +
    labs(title = "Montgomery County Crime Trend", y = "Incidents of Crime", 
         x = "Year") +
    geom_line()
```

```{r Plot of incidents per 100K people}
#Displays the incidents of Crime 100K people

Data.3 %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x=YEAR, y=(GRAND.TOTAL*100000)/POPULATION)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(title = "Montgomery County", y="Crime Per 100,000")
```

```{r Crime types over time}
#Displays a lines graph that shows property & violent crime over time.
#While violent crimes, which are relatively low, remained constant, but a steep
#drop in property crimes has occurred in recent times.

Data.3 %>% 
    select(YEAR,VIOLENT.CRIME.TOTAL,PROPERTY.CRIME.TOTALS) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = c(VIOLENT.CRIME.TOTAL, PROPERTY.CRIME.TOTALS), names_to = "Type.of.Crime", values_to = "Amount.of.Crime") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x=YEAR, y=Amount.of.Crime, colour = Type.of.Crime)) +
    geom_line()
```

## IX. Incorporating Machine Learning Techniques

There was an article on medium.com, that detailed how a Boosting Machine
Learning Algorithm could be used to Predict Neighborhood Safety in a
specific neighborhood in June 2019 by Babak Shahian Jahromi. It spoke of
a project that created a web application using a predictive machine
learning approach that could find the criminal hotspots as well as the
location and time of committed crimes. It could receive an address or
location in Chicago and predict the probability of crime at a specific
location at a particular time. Further, it would show incidents and mark
it on a map highlighting areas. Therefore, it would be useful to
incorporate such a model to answer my research questions in a similar
manner.

Their approach was to take historical data from an area over a specified
period of time. Then, the data was preprocessed by dropping duplicates
and parsing dates and times into similar components. Next the data was
balanced with similar counts between reports where an arrest was made vs
no arrest made. The data was then trained and tested into an 80/20. Then
the analyst modeled using Logistic Regression, Naïve Bayes, Support
Vector Machines, K-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Trees, Random Forest, and
XG-Boosting. Finally, the web application was loaded with two options.
One to enter the location and datetime into a specified format and
clicking a “is it safe?” button. And the other option was to enter the
address desired and clicking the “find the crimes” button.

## X. Questions for Future Steps

One of the major questions that I had hoped to address was to determine
if people were moving to or away from the county as I had presumed that
if it were unsafe, people would find other places to live. But I began
to realize that the population numbers would not be enough to make this
determination. It would be more useful to use other types of data, for
example, out-of-state moving trucks, or reports from moving companies
bring people into or out of the area.\
Furthermore, birth and death rates would affect the population numbers.
I wish I had a better idea of how to choose the necessary variable
needed for analysis into a particular subject. It is my guess that only
time and experience will support this effort.

# Part THREE

## I.	Introduction

The focus for this research project is to determine if Montgomery County 
Maryland is a relatively safe place in which to live. To gather the information 
needed, statistics to be considered will come from the Census Bureau; data from 
the Montgomery County Crime Data as collected from the United States General 
Services Agency’s website; as well as information from the Open Data Portal on 
the State of Maryland government website. The intent is to show that when 
compared to the size of the population in relation to the number of reported 
incidents of violent crimes, as well as property crimes, one will be able to 
decide if it is safe enough to live in the county. 


## II.	Problem Statement Addressed

Several questions will be addressed in this report using visuals on comparisons 
that will answer a few supporting questions.

1.	How was safety defined? Safety was measured in the number of incidents of 
crimes toward persons and property per capita as compared to other places.
2.	How much crime? By collecting the number of incidents by individual 
neighborhoods in Montgomery County, one would incorrectly determine that 
Montgomery County has a lot of crime. This report presents a table as well as a 
bar chart that shows that if you only consider the number of incidents as 
compared to other places, Montgomery County looks as if it is one of the most 
dangerous counties in the State. But the chart that takes the size and 
population into account, one can see that it is a very safe county.
3.	How has crime trended? Montgomery County has seen a steep decline in overall 
crime, but especially crimes against property.


## III.	How Problem Statement was Addressed

In order to assist someone to determine the level of safety, it was necessary to 
combine several files of data into a usable format that will allow analysis that 
can locate the incidents of crime, the types of crimes, as well as how recent it 
was committed. This is important because using data from ten years ago would not 
be especially useful for what may be happening today. So, combining information 
from datasets, condensing it down to eliminate reports that may not necessarily 
determine the security of an area (for example driving under the influence) were 
excluded. The goal was to clean the data so that it could be set up to use in 
several analysis tools. One method that may be useful could be the K-means 
Algorithm. In this analysis one could find where clusters of specific crimes 
occur. Because “safe” is a term that everyone defines according to their 
experiences and impressions, seeing the different clusters may give insights 
that other methods may not implore.

One of the methods used in this report was descriptive analysis. Crime was 
calculated per one hundred thousand people. The reasoning for this is that a 
percent change only explains a portion of what is going on when you compare 
items. When you take a ‘per capita’ value, it allows you to make a comparison 
analysis amongst groupings of varied sizes. The per capita value is determined 
by dividing the number of incidents of crime by the total population in the 
area. With this method, one can see that although the number of crimes has risen 
over the last decade, there has been an overall drop in crime during the same 
period. Analysis of the population also shows a rise during this time, which 
would explain the rise in the numbers. Generally, if there are more people in 
an area, it makes sense that there would be more criminal activity. Ultimately, 
this method allowed me to make an apples-to-apples determination of the security 
levels of towns of all sizes within Maryland and where Montgomery County is 
placed in that categorization.


## IV.	Analysis

When the research for this project began, the assumption was that Montgomery 
County is riddled with crime, given the overwhelming look of the first map with 
the legend that differentiates the diverse types of crime, and being less than 
30 miles from the notoriously dangerous Baltimore. Yet, as we moved through the 
comparative analysis to the surrounding areas (even outside Maryland) it 
revealed the true state of criminal activity within the county borders. It 
dropped when looking at the sheer number of crimes, but per capita and trend 
examinations helped to display the more accurate picture - it came out less 
than a third the rate of the city of Baltimore. {It would be of further interest 
to me to break these numbers down into types of crime and even the time of day 
that these occurred.} 

Another surprise was how Montgomery County stacked up against counties of the 
same sized population. It had one of the lowest crime rates, as shown on the 
scatterplot in green. 

Furthermore, the trend of incidents per 100k people was enlightening. During the 
same period (1975-2020) crime rose and fell with a double high peak around 1991 
and 1995. But the peak of per 100K analysis shows a steady decline during this 
period with its peak occurring in 1980.

Finally, the most stunning insight was that violent crimes remained low at a 
steady rate over the last four decades even though population has risen over 
time.


## V.	Implications

It is then implied that although no one can guarantee the statistics will play 
out in real life, Montgomery County, compared to the surrounding areas within 
the state of Maryland, is a safe place to live given its size and downward trend 
in rate of incidents. 

Also, not explicitly clear is that there has been a redefining of what is 
classified as a crime over the recent years. Nearly all crime stats are 
published by the FBI and the Bureau of Justice Statistics, and only those crimes 
that are reported to law enforcement are included in these reports. Also, the 
data only includes a handful of specific violent and property crimes but does 
not always include crimes such as drug offenses. Furthermore, not all law 
enforcement agencies participate in the collection process each year.


## VI.	Limitations

One limitation of this research paper was the lack of expertise for the analyst. 
As this is only the third of ten courses within the study of Data Analysis (and 
the first-time using R), much more is possible to aid in answering the key 
question, ‘Is Montgomery County Maryland a Safe Place to Live.’ There is much 
more that could be done with the same premise and data, had this project been 
assigned later in the program of study.

Other limitations of any analysis of crime rates are the fact that many crimes 
are under-reported or reported incorrectly. (For example, in one of the 
datasets, city names were misspelled and thus were misplaced.) Also, 
jurisdictions categorize crimes differently and have varied practices.

The aforementioned machine learning example could make the analysis more 
relevant by allowing a user-defined approach as well as up-to-the-minute output. 
The example was user friendly and allowed for multiple ways to recall the data – 
by pushing the “is it safe” button or “find the crimes” button. 

One may even use an ANOVA method to assess differences in average crime rates in 
Montgomery County and the average rates in another like sized neighborhood.


## VII.	Concluding Remarks

It was great to see that Montgomery County (the most populous county in 
Maryland) showed a decline in crime over the last decade. Surrounding areas like 
DC, Baltimore, and Price George’s County have all seen rises in overall crime. 
Yet though there was an increase in population, unlawful acts, 
uncharacteristically, showed a sharp reduction. The data collected was useful 
because it collected specific crimes, where they were committed, and where the 
activities were reported. While there is room to expand this analysis in this 
report, it was sufficient to provide evidentiary details to allow one to access 
the level of safety one would experience moving to Montgomery County.
